---
title: "Python interface"
---

The Python package `denmark` mirrors the R package function by function. It grids the cells in the same order, builds the same Stan data and fits the same Stan models through [cmdstanpy](https://mc-stan.org/cmdstanpy/), so results from the two languages are directly comparable. Tests check that both build the same Stan data from the toy data, with and without the tissue boundary.

## Installation

```bash
pip install "git+https://github.com/StaGill/DenMark#subdirectory=python"
python -m cmdstanpy.install_cmdstan
```

`denmark` needs Python 3.9 or later with numpy 1.21, pandas 1.3, scipy 1.7 and cmdstanpy 1.2 or later. Three extras are optional: `boundary` adds shapely (2.0 or later) for the tissue boundary, `plot` adds matplotlib (3.5 or later) for the figures, and `test` adds pytest (7.0 or later).

```bash
pip install "denmark[boundary,plot] @ git+https://github.com/StaGill/DenMark#subdirectory=python"
```

`python -m cmdstanpy.install_cmdstan` downloads and builds CmdStan once per machine and needs a C++ toolchain.

## Quick start

```python
import denmark as dm

toy = dm.datasets.load_toy()
tissue = dm.alpha_shape(toy["x"], toy["y"])   # tissue boundary from all cells
tumor = toy[toy["celltype"] == "Tumor"].drop(columns="celltype")
res = dm.DenMark(tumor, gene="geneA", boundary=tissue, grid_size=10, basis=10,
                 chains=2, iter_warmup=500, iter_sampling=500, seed=2024)
print(res)
```

`dm.denmark` is a lowercase alias of `dm.DenMark`. A fit returns a `DenMarkResult`, whose methods take the place of the R post-processing functions.

## R and Python side by side

| Task | R | Python |
|---|---|---|
| Gene filter | `denmark_filter_genes(expr)` | `filter_genes(expr)` |
| Tissue boundary | `denmark_alpha_shape(x, y)` | `alpha_shape(x, y)` |
| Grid | `buildgridpp(grid_size, dataset, gene)` | `buildgridpp(grid_size, dataset, gene)` |
| Grid centroids | `grid_pts_centroid(grid_size, dataset)` | `grid_pts_centroid(grid_size, dataset)` |
| HSGP basis indices | `denmark_hsgp_indices(basis)` | `hsgp_indices(basis)` |
| Stan data | `denmark_prepare()` | `prepare_data()` |
| Compile a model | `denmark_model()` | `compile_model()` |
| Initial values | `denmark_init()`, which returns a function | `make_init()`, which returns a dict |
| Fit one gene | `DenMark()`, `DenMarkmain()` | `DenMark()` or `denmark()`, `DenMarkmain()` |
| Posterior summary | `denmark_summary(fit)` | `res.summary()` |
| Harmonized draws | `denmark_draws(fit)` | `res.draws()`, `res.rho` |
| Latent fields | `denmark_fields(fit)` | `res.fields()` |
| Correlation decay | `denmark_decay(fit)` | `res.decay()` |
| HSGP check | `denmark_check_hsgp(fit)` | `res.check_hsgp()` |
| Gene scan | `denmark_scan()` | `scan_genes()` |
| Save and reload | `denmark_save()`, `denmark_load()` (RDS) | `save_result()`, `load_result()` (pickle) |
| Simulation | `denmark_simulate()` | `simulate()` |
| Toy data | `denmark_toy_data()` | `denmark.datasets.load_toy()` |
| Figures | `plot_denmark_boundary()`, `plot_denmark_grid()`, `plot_denmark_fields()`, `plot_denmark_decay()`, `plot_denmark_scan()` (ggplot2) | `plot_boundary()`, `plot_grid()`, `plot_fields()`, `plot_decay()`, `plot_scan()` (matplotlib figures) |
| Matérn-3/2 covariance | `matern32(d, sigma, rho)` | `matern32(d, sigma, ell)` |

## Differences to keep in mind

- Grid indices start at 1 in R (`grid_index = i + (j - 1) * nx`) and at 0 in Python (`grid_index = i + j * nx`). In both, x varies fastest.
- The tissue boundary is an sf polygon with the attribute `alpha` in R and a `TissueBoundary` in Python, whose `.polygon` is a shapely polygon and whose `.alpha` and `.area` hold the alpha and the tissue area. Both languages take it as `boundary` in the same functions.
- A few arguments have different names: `DenMark()` takes `inits` in Python and `init` in R, and `compile_model()` takes `force_compile` where `denmark_model()` takes `force_recompile`. The plot functions take `xlabel` and `ylabel` where R takes `xlab` and `ylab`, and `point_size` in `plot_boundary()` is a matplotlib marker area in points squared rather than a ggplot2 point size.
- With a tissue boundary, the grid areas agree between the languages up to the last bit: sf computes polygon areas with GDAL's formula and shapely with GEOS's. Grid indices, types, counts and coordinates are identical.
- The third argument of `matern32()` is the length-scale in both languages. R calls it `rho` for backward compatibility; it is not the density-expression correlation.
- `simulate()` draws with numpy's generator, so it does not reproduce `denmark_simulate()` for the same seed. To compare the two languages on the same data, read the same file, as the toy data do.
- With `save_dir`, `scan_genes()` caches one CSV row per gene and `denmark_scan()` one RDS file per gene, so an interrupted scan resumes where it stopped.
- `keep_fit=False` keeps only the draws of the key parameters, which saves memory in large scans; `res.fields()` then needs a refit.

## A full analysis

```python
import os
import tempfile

import denmark as dm

toy = dm.datasets.load_toy()
tumor = toy[toy["celltype"] == "Tumor"].drop(columns="celltype")

# Tissue boundary: alpha shape of all cells, not only the Tumor cells
tissue = dm.alpha_shape(toy["x"], toy["y"])
print(tissue.alpha, tissue.area)

# Grid: cell counts Y and summed expression M per grid, with x varying fastest;
# with a boundary, each grid is interior, boundary or exterior
g = dm.buildgridpp(10, tumor, gene="geneA", boundary=tissue)
fig = dm.plot_boundary(toy, tissue, grid=g, highlight=toy["celltype"] == "Tumor")
fig = dm.plot_grid(g)

# Stan data: the grids inside the tissue, centered on the region, with one log area each;
# HSGP basis functions and boundary factor
prep = dm.prepare_data(tumor, gene="geneA", grid_size=10, basis=10, boundfactor=1.5,
                       boundary=tissue)
print(sorted(prep["stan_data"]))

# Fit the model
fit = dm.DenMark(tumor, gene="geneA", boundary=tissue, grid_size=10, basis=10,
                 chains=2, iter_warmup=500, iter_sampling=500, seed=2024)

# Interpret: draws of rho and of a11, a21, a22; latent fields; spatial correlation decay
draws = fit.draws()
print(draws["rho"].quantile([0.025, 0.5, 0.975]))
fig = dm.plot_fields(fit)
print(fit.decay()["ranges"])
fig = dm.plot_decay(fit)
print(fit.check_hsgp())

# Screen genes: PCG if the 95% credible interval of rho lies above 0, NCG if below 0
scan = dm.scan_genes(tumor, boundary=tissue, grid_size=10, basis=10, chains=2,
                     iter_warmup=500, iter_sampling=500, seed=2024)
print(scan[["gene", "rho_mean", "rho_lower", "rho_upper", "class"]])
fig = dm.plot_scan(scan)

# Keep a fit for a later session (the CmdStan output files are temporary)
path = os.path.join(tempfile.gettempdir(), "denmark_geneA.pkl")
dm.save_result(fit, path)
fit = dm.load_result(path)
```

## Your own data

Start from one row per cell of the section, with coordinates `x`, `y`, the cell type and raw counts, one column per gene. The tissue boundary uses all cells; the model uses the cells of the focal population:

```python
import pandas as pd
import denmark as dm

cells = pd.read_csv("cells.csv")   # columns x, y, celltype and one count column per gene
tissue = dm.alpha_shape(cells["x"], cells["y"])
focal = cells[cells["celltype"] == "Tumor"].drop(columns="celltype")
genes = dm.filter_genes(focal.drop(columns=["x", "y"]))
res = dm.DenMark(focal, gene=genes[0], boundary=tissue, grid_size=30)
```

## Stan models

The package ships byte-identical copies of the Stan models in the R package's `inst/stan/` and compiles them on first use in a user cache directory, since the installed package may be read-only. The directory is set by the environment variable `DENMARK_CACHE_DIR` and defaults to `~/.cache/denmark`. With `boundary`, `DenMark()` fits `DenMark-vararea.stan`, the same model with one area offset per grid cell. `DenMark(stan_file=...)` fits a custom Stan file, which must declare the same data and parameters as `DenMark.stan`, or as `DenMark-vararea.stan` when a boundary is given.
